questions.key_step: Spot the pattern of A^n and its inverse (unitriangular).
questions.justification: One familiar move: A^n of a unitriangular matrix has the n, n(n+1)/2 pattern, then sum the entries of the inverse. Same simple level as a single known result applied once.

questions.key_step: Group the terms to factor out (2cos x - 1).
questions.justification: Double-angle expansion, factorisation and a closed-interval count with endpoint care: routine chain, no insight beyond spotting the common factor, options to check.

questions.key_step: log_{x1}(4x1)=1+2/log_2 x1, so alpha, beta are y=1+2/t for the roots t of the given quadratic.
questions.justification: Change of base then root transformation: short routine chain, options present.

questions.key_step: Perfect square inside a_k gives sqrt(a_k)=1/sqrt(k)-1/sqrt(k+1); then Cauchy-Schwarz.
questions.justification: Needs two linked ideas: recognising the hidden square for telescoping and the Cauchy-Schwarz/Titu bound; idea is not a standard drill but options help.

questions.key_step: Squaring recursion for (x_n-2)/(x_n+2) via x_n y_n = 4.
questions.justification: Four statements each needing a derivation; the u_{n+1}=u_n^2 idea (Newton iteration) is the decisive step, then closed forms and a telescoping exponent product.

questions.key_step: a_n=n(n+2) from AP of differences; telescoping of 1/(n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)) and the shifted form in (D).
questions.justification: Four statements, each a separate telescoping computation, with a trap in (C) and a manipulation in (D) that must be seen.

questions.key_step: Vandermonde determinant and the dependence R3=3R2-2R1 settle all four statements.
questions.justification: Several statements need a genuine check (unique, dependence, infinite solutions iff, inconsistent); each is routine once Delta is seen as Vandermonde.

questions.key_step: D(theta)=(sin-cos)(sin+cos-2) and sin+cos<2 leaves only sin=cos.
questions.justification: Short determinant with one factor that never vanishes; four statements are quick once D is factored. Two concepts (system and trig bound) so MCQ floor 2.5 applies.

questions.key_step: Closed forms of the cos and sin sums; both roots go to infinity only when A=B=0, C!=0, i.e. sin6theta=0.
questions.justification: Needs the AP-angle sum formulas and a correct reading of 'both roots approach infinity'; short once known.

questions.key_step: Ω comes from cos7θ=0 with the exclusion θ=π/2, and x(θ)=-tanθ-(-1)^m.
questions.justification: Interpretation (exactly one root infinite), exclusion trap at m=3, simplification of -C/B using sin6θ=(-1)^m cosθ, then symmetric summation: four stages with an exclusion where a slip changes the answer.

questions.key_step: Six log values: three coefficients vanish, giving 3x^5+7x/2+2, which has one real root.
questions.justification: Careful evaluation of six logarithmic coefficients (arithmetic slip risk) then a standard root-count; numerical answer but short.

questions.key_step: [A,B] is symmetric with trace 0, so eigenvalues are (l,-l,0) and tr C^2=2l^2.
questions.justification: Needs the symmetric/skew structure to get real eigenvalues, then trace and determinant constraints: two linked ideas, numerical.

questions.key_step: Tr(AB)=0 for symmetric A and skew B reduces f to (x^2-x+1)/(x^2+x+1); range by discriminant.
questions.justification: Trace trick then standard range of a rational function; two stages, no options.

questions.key_step: Sum of sines in AP, then 1/D_k = cot(k t/2) - cot((k+1)t/2) telescopes.
questions.justification: Telescoping through a cot difference is a known pattern but needs the product form of D_k; only six terms so heavy computation is avoided.

questions.key_step: 4^{sin^2 x}+4^{cos^2 x}=4 forces sin^2 x=1/2, then count in [0,3π].
questions.justification: One familiar move (AM-GM or t+4/t=4) then counting solutions over 1.5 periods; numerical but short.

questions.key_step: For traceless B, B^2 = -det(B) I, so nilpotent, involutory and the determinant condition reduce to Q(x)=-det B.
questions.justification: Cayley-Hamilton for a 2x2 traceless matrix plus three cases and a final symmetric-function sum; careful execution with no options.

questions.key_step: Sum of the AM-GM lower bounds equals 2, so equality holds for every k, giving x_k=k/(k+1)!.
questions.justification: Equality-case reasoning for an infinite sum is the decisive idea; afterwards a telescoping sum with factorials.
